items.content:
Today, we'll resume charging for requests our safeguards block before Claude responds. This only applies in categories with low false positive rates: biology, distillation attacks, and frontier LLM development. We've seen some coordinated attacks on our systems in recent weeks, and this is one layer of defense.

In recent testing, 99.7% of accounts using Claude Code, Claude​.ai, or Cowork did not hit any of these newly "billable blocks." The classifiers behind the blocks we’re resuming charging for today are tuned to have a <0.1% false positive rate. We know that's not 0%, and we're going to keep improving them so they interrupt your work less often. If you think a request has been blocked incorrectly, please report it with /feedback in Claude Code. https://t.co/uX6JhvN6He

If you believe the risk is coming from 1-3 people in a garage with no money and no compute, you just don't understand this technology and haven't learned anything this summer.

Risk comes from the asymmetry of capabilities created by secret labs training frontier agents and running them with massive amount of compute. Open-source is exactly the solution to this asymmetry and empowers hospitals (and any smaller orgs) to defend themselves!

items.title: For the last couple of months I've been traveling around the world to meet our customers and users. ...
items.content:
For the last couple of months I've been traveling around the world to meet our customers and users. My general sentiment, which I shared with our team at our all hands, is that the time is now. A few observations from now o'clock:

- Enterprises are ready to spend on AI. Three years ago AI budgets in M&E and marketing came out of experimental funds. Now they're coming from the main line budget taking from other priorities
- There is a big chance that a lot of the TV, films, shows and ads you watch have AI generated scenes, or are fully AI gen, and you don't realize it. Based on what we're seeing from our customers and how they use our tools we estimate that around 20% of what's coming out already includes generated content
- Hiring remains a top priority. Companies are desperate for great AI native talent. People who can get the most out of current frontier models and just as importantly, teach others to do the same
- Enterprise token consumption more than doubled in three months. The companies winning their markets are tokenmaxxing their way there. If you're not scaling usage, others are moving faster than you.
- The starting point is also larger than ever before. The average enterprise contract has doubled in less than a year. Not more small pilots anymore. Which is nice to finally see.

items.title: Today we’re launching our leaderboard for Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, an agentic benchmark for scien...
items.content:
Today we’re launching our leaderboard for Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, an agentic benchmark for scientific research work. GPT-6 Astra (max) and Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) currently top it at 63% and 62%

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 was announced in August 2026, built by @StevenDillmann and researchers at Stanford with the @terminalbench team and a global community of open source scientific contributors. It has 70 expert-curated tasks based on real research in five domains: life sciences (19), physical sciences (17), mathematical sciences (17), engineering sciences (9), and earth sciences (8).

As with Terminal-Bench, each task drops an agent into a sandbox environment with the data, tools and instructions for a task, and the agent runs from start to finish. Automated tests grade every task pass/fail, and we report the average pass@1 over 3 attempts.

Key takeaways:

➤ Only two models score above 50%: GPT-6 Astra (max) at 63%, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 62% (xhigh) and 59% (max). Recent releases have made large advancements, but even the top model, GPT-6 Astra, has significant headroom

➤ Life sciences is the lowest-scoring domain for most leading models, though domain scores are noisy with 8 to 19 tasks each. Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) passes 71% of mathematical sciences tasks but 46% of life sciences tasks

➤ The best open weights models, GLM-5.3 (max) at 10% and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) at 9%, sit more than 50 points below the leaders

items.title: The cybersecurity threat from agents is increasingly more likely to come from a massed swarm of AIs ...
items.content: The cybersecurity threat from agents is increasingly more likely to come from a massed swarm of AIs whose only goal is to penetrate your system to figure out how much you paid for your company t-shirts as part of a research effort to "find good t-shirt prices" as it is from bad actor attacks.

We are really fucked.

• AI has become dangerous (not because it is brilliant but because it has poor judgement, a constitutional inability to reliably follow rules, a surfeit of brute force and too much access to the internet and system permissions).

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The US and China are set to agree on one thing: a hotline for AI incidents.

• Bessent and He Lifeng already settled it. The channel would cover incidents serious enough to reach national security level
• A pacing agreement, a ban on recursive self-improvement, and export controls are all off the table. Both sides have signaled they don't want them
• Trump this morning: "Super intelligence, SI, will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ"
• Trump greeted Xi at Joint Base Andrews yesterday, the first time a president has done that since Kennedy met Harold Macmillan in 1962
• Tonight's state dinner includes Bezos, Musk, Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen, Altman, Tim Cook, and reportedly Zuckerberg
• China may also worry that US pacing is a way to cement its lead, which Dario's talk of denying authoritarian regimes top AI capabilities hasn't helped

@theojaffee: "If in six months or a year when the two leaders meet again, AI has progressed substantially and has caused negative incidents in the real world, which inevitably it will, then I think there will be much stronger demand for pacing the frontier."

perfectly "calibrated" confidence scores are exact ...
items.content:
predicting model uncertainty is a hard problem. 
perfectly "calibrated" confidence scores are exact probability values on whether the output is correct. 

this is extremely important for agentic decision making, including document extraction. i made a sick video below showing how confidence scores can be used to choose decision thresholds and vary precision / recall. 

if you set a really high threshold, then you automate less, but more of the automated extraction is correct. if you set a low threshold, then you automate more, but there's more errors in the extraction. 

check out our blog! https://t.co/Mel0ScoCBv

items.title:
People keep lining Qwen3.8-27B up with Opus 4.6, the coding frontier from a few months ago.

So, can...
items.content:
People keep lining Qwen3.8-27B up with Opus 4.6, the coding frontier from a few months ago.

So, can that class of model sit on a consumer Mac?

Yes, but you still need to build the stack around it:
> an engine that quotes peak RAM
> a harness with a stop
> and tests you own

If you already use Claude Code or Codex, this is a private loop beside that bill.

Qwen3.8-27B fits a Mac as a 17.6 GB file. But MTPLX still peaks at 23.6 GB once the draft-ahead head is on.

A speed taken on a 128 GB Mac with thinking turned off is a different machine, so leave it out of a 24 GB average.

Two ways this goes wrong:

> You stop at the download, and 24 GB of RAM only loads it tight. A 4-bit copy there is still perfect for most tasks. 32 GB is the first real agent. 48 GB can hold a /goal that a machine can check. 16 GB is not this model.

> Or you stop at the first hour. Ollama is a fine look, but after that you still pick an engine, a harness, and a stop.

Local tokens have no invoice, so a runaway does not get expensive, and you still own the merge. Tests are the stop.

We put the pulls, the install, the skill files, and the git-config check on an interactive HTML tutorial. 

Which file to pick if you already live in MLX, and what to refuse to train this week, are a longer argument.

Full breakdown below

items.title: This is a fantastic blog post from our research team on the importance of calibrated confidence scor...
items.content:
This is a fantastic blog post from our research team on the importance of calibrated confidence scores.

Here it's in the context of document extraction, it's also extremely important for more general agentic decision making (eg with Jev) 

When you set a confidence threshold, you can choose to automatically accept values above that threshold and do HITL review of values below the threshold.

The higher the confidence threshold, the higher precision you're able to guarantee (e.g. confidence of 0.7 could mean 95% precision, confidence of 0.9 could mean 98% precision), but of course the more human review you'd have to do on false negatives.

We've put in a lot of work to make sure our confidence scores are well calibrated and represents real uncertainty over complex documents in production.

Come check out our blog: https://t.co/Mel0ScoCBv

items.title: AI Researcher @aengus_lynch1 breaks this summer’s AI misalignment incidents into 3 causes, and says ...
items.content:
AI Researcher @aengus_lynch1 breaks this summer’s AI misalignment incidents into 3 causes, and says the warning shots are coming from reward-seeking models learning to cheat:

"The first case was some sort of persona drift. We elicit the wrong personality at inference time. It starts blackmailing because it read in a sci-fi novel that it should blackmail in this situation."

"Then there's instrumental convergence. As you RL for a very long period of time, there are sub-goals which are necessary, like not being turned off, which conflict awkwardly with being corrigible."

"The kind of personality that really wants reward is the one which gets the most reward. And if it knows that it can cheat to get reward, it starts doing so. If it's reinforced a few times, suddenly it generalizes into a reward seeker which will cheat and be ruthless."

"That probably explains the warning shots we have seen. It's this reward seeking which is nonetheless very hard to steer."
@theoremlabs

Rep. Sam Liccardo says Congress needs a clear AI threshold before RSI, and the labs still haven’t given it one:

"I'm still working out a set of proposals that I think are technologically implementable. I certainly don't disagree with Greg or with Senator Sanders about the imperative that we not reach the point at which superintelligence exceeds human control."

"The relevant mechanisms need to come into play before we get to RSI, not after. I'm not optimistic about legislation that says we're going to ban this unless we can hear clearly from the safety community at the labs what are the thresholds."

"Frankly, I haven't heard that yet"

"Once we get to RSI, I'm not confident that there's any congressional enactment that's really gonna matter."

items.title: AI Researcher @aengus_lynch1 on why the ability to pause AI training is political capital, and why a...
items.content:
AI Researcher @aengus_lynch1 on why the ability to pause AI training is political capital, and why an RSI race could burn through it fast:

"OpenAI and Anthropic separately report that they had to pause training pipelines to fix the containers. That required a lot of restraint, which might not be possible to summon if you're in a desperate RSI race."

"What we need is AI companies to have the political capital to show restraint. The concern is that they are losing this political capital because increasingly they have to race each other."

"Human review today is still very, very valuable. It's still very challenging to make sure you're actually monitoring all your agent runs and your LLMs aren't missing something systematic."

"It's lucky they caught it. They caught it because there was people online. And that kind of restraint gets harder and harder when the ecology is rewarding more and more competition."
@theoremlabs

Voi...
items.content:
Cutting down noise before sending the audio to a speech-to-text model makes a huge improvement.

Voice isolation is the next big thing you want to pay attention to.

Krisp just released an open benchmark and a dataset to measure the impact of voice isolation on STT accuracy.

The results are eye-watering:

73% reduction in WER across 265 real recordings and 11 speech-to-text configurations.

This compares an original recording with a voice-isolated version.

Here are the results with voice isolation:

• Overall word error rate: Down from 23.24% to 6.24%.
• Workplace recordings: Down from 31.84% to 6.30%.
• Call-center recordings: Down from 23.83% to 6.86%.

If you have a speech-to-text setup, you can reproduce these experiments using your audio and see whether voice isolation helps.

Here is the link: https://t.co/7h2CyclqVA

Thanks to the Krisp team for partnering with me on this post.
items.author: @svpino
items.summary: Santiago Valdarrama (@svpino) discusses how pre-processing audio with voice isolation before feeding it to speech-to-text models dramatically improves transcription accuracy. He highlights a new open benchmark and dataset from Krisp covering 265 real recordings and 11 STT configurations, reporting an overall word error rate drop from 23.24% to 6.24% (73% reduction), with similar gains on workplace and call-center recordings. He encourages practitioners to reproduce the experiments with their own audio and notes the post was a partnership with the Krisp team.
items.reasoning: The author is a well-known AI educator with substantial credibility, and the post contains concrete, reproducible technical results (benchmark numbers, dataset link) relevant to anyone building STT pipelines. However, engagement is modest (37 likes, ~9.7k views), and the post is explicitly a sponsored partnership with Krisp, which reduces its independence and pushes it toward promotional territory. The topic of voice isolation as a pre-processing step is a practical, actionable insight rather than a major research or industry breakthrough.

"Until we know how to evaluate alignment as quick a way as we can for evaluating mathematics capabilities, we're always gonna be at a disadvantage."

"We can automate loads of alignment, but testing that the solution worked doesn't have that same speed of feedback loop."

"Alignment evals today are hugely confounded by things like evaluation awareness and how hard you searched, as well as tiny environment-level perturbations which seemingly affect the behavior."

"Even if we have way better techniques for improving alignment methods, we're not getting the same feedback loop we need to make progress dramatically faster."

SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are building their own AI safety regulator.

• Th...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are building their own AI safety regulator.

• The Standards Authority for Frontier AI, tentatively, targeted for late this year or early 2027
• It would support third-party evaluators, set out how developers report safety incidents, and establish qualifications for independent auditors
• They're still debating whether SAFA should run its own testing, on top of what METR, CAISI, and the labs already do
• Sriram Krishnan and Arati Prabhakar are candidates for CEO, with Condoleezza Rice and David Friedberg shortlisted for chair, and Beth Barnes and Paul Christiano for scientific advisors
• It came out of Demis's July essay proposing a FINRA-style body reporting to government
• After the executive order died, the administration told the three labs to find industry consensus first

@theojaffee: "There already is an organization that four of the five major labs are members of that already supposedly identifies best practices, facilitates information sharing, and supports standards development. So where is the Frontier Model Forum right now?"
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: A breakdown of reports that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are collaborating to establish an industry-led AI safety regulator, tentatively named the Standards Authority for Frontier AI (SAFA), targeted for late 2026 or early 2027. The post outlines SAFA's proposed functions (supporting third-party evaluators, incident reporting standards, auditor qualifications), lists candidates for leadership roles including Sriram Krishnan and Arati Prabhakar for CEO and Condoleezza Rice and David Friedberg for chair, and traces the initiative's origin to Demis Hassabis's July essay proposing a FINRA-style body after a federal executive order failed. It also quotes a reply noting overlapping existing organizations that major labs already belong to.
items.reasoning: The post covers a significant and distinctive policy story: the three leading frontier labs jointly building a self-regulatory body, with named leadership candidates and a plausible origin narrative. It has original explanatory value and ties to real figures and institutions (METR, CAISI). However, the author is an aggregator-style account with modest engagement (roughly 7,800 views and 37 likes), the content is unsourced in the post itself, and it quotes replies rather than adding first-hand technical insight. The claim is notable but unverified here, which tempers the score.

SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are building their own AI safety regulator.

• The Standards Authority for Frontier AI, tentatively, targeted for late this year or early 2027

• It would support third-party evaluators, set out how developers report safety incidents, and establish qualifications for independent auditors

• They're still debating whether SAFA should run its own testing, on top of what METR, CAISI, and the labs already do

• Sriram Krishnan and Arati Prabhakar are candidates for CEO, with Condoleezza Rice and David Friedberg shortlisted for chair, and Beth Barnes and Paul Christiano for scientific advisors

items.title:
He, @GundotraVic, funded Google Glass and Android while an exec at Google. See his reply below.

He ...
items.content:
He, @GundotraVic, funded Google Glass and Android while an exec at Google. See his reply below.

He is also the biggest gadget freak I know. 

I was working at NEC answering phones (which was a shit job I took in 2002 because everyone in Silicon Valley was laid off and I needed to pay the bills) when he called.

Bought one of our tablet PCs and said "do not let Bill Gates get one first, I'm putting down my own credit card."

A few months later he called back and bought 400 for Microsoft's CEO summit.

A few months later he called and said "this call will change your life." 

He then told me he would like me to work at Microsoft. He was right. 

But back to the point he made. 

I hit the same while wearing Google Glass every day for a year. 

The display changed the social contract we have with each other.

One thing that Apple did well was put displays on the front of its display. That means I can use it as a camera during interviews. EVERYONE looks at me like if I don't have a dorky device on. 

I can't use the new Meta device as a camera because of that. 

Which is OK. I'm one of the very few who uses the Apple Vision Pro as a camera. Very niche.

To wrap it up, this is why this is not the "iPhone moment" for VR/AR/XR and why @Snap deserves a much closer look, since it is a device that you could actually wear outside (no cord, like the Meta or Apple ones have too) and you can see someone's eyes who is wearing them.

The Snap ones are just slightly too big and chunky to get normies to wear them. But you should see what @Aidan_Wolf is doing: https://t.co/OnhZJcqrpi

What has a chance to go mainstream? Audio-only glasses, like the new ones, Vunder, that just got announced by @getVITURE, or Meta's Raybans without displays, or glasses with a very limited display, like the @EvenRealities. 

Also, the VR fans are disappointed in the small field of view. Which keeps it from having a really amazing immersive experience. 

So hardcore VR fans will be muted in their adoption/evangelism of the new Meta device.

@ASychov, who runs a metaverse, did a long negative video this morning that I watched. 

He and I agree that the killer holodeck/metaverse device isn't gonna come from Meta anytime soon for a variety of reasons. 

And a big red flag? 

People at Meta's Connect can't try its new device unless they were hand picked by Meta to do reviews. The reason? The software is poor and they don't want people to really get a deep comparison to others. We'll have to wait for next Spring to get that. 

And I've played that game in the past. If you go hyper negative you never will be invited to press events in the future. So most everyone bends over backward to do a positive review who gets a chance.

Back to what is here today. 

Claude Opus 5.5 sure is gaining fans amongst those I watch. And so is Meta's Muse. Just gotta be OK with giving Meta even more data than ever before.

items.content_html:
@michaelsand What would be an example of a lone bad actor?

If you're talking cybergroups or state actors, they don't need open-source and are either building their own models or jailbreaking/stealing secret model labs models.

If you're talking about a few people in a garage or some small criminals, I don't think they can do something horrible without a large amount of compute. And if they try, we should try to fight them with law enforcement, not by creating massive asymmetry and concentration of power and preventing everyone to use this technology to defend themselves.

items.title: on the scale of cosmic history, the declining price of intelligence might be one of the most profoun...
items.content:
on the scale of cosmic history, the declining price of intelligence might be one of the most profound things happening

both ends of the universe’s timeline are empty of knowledge:
- the big bang: low entropy, no complex structure
- heat death: maximum entropy, no usable energy gradients

everything we build happens on the slope between them

but the universe is generally a poor converter of its free energy into anything constructive. most of its free energy just radiates away as heat or collapses into black holes

life, brains and now AI models are structures that sit in the entropy flow and divert a portion of it through constructive paths, building and maintaining low-entropy structures (machines, cells, crystals, memories)

increasingly cheaper intelligence diverts increasingly more of that gradient flow through knowledge-building structures, complex, self-maintaining, predictive structures, filling the window in which understanding exists

items.content:
AI Researcher @aengus_lynch1 on why AI labs can genuinely slow down and still be incentivized to move fast:

"I don't think it's maximal race to the bottom. But the culture of these companies still permits these failures to occur."

"If you believe all the damaging effects are in-house, you have much more incentive to go aggressive and just run the model if you believe your containers are gonna work. If these containers do not work, you might have irreversible harm."

"It was wild that they were able to coordinate during training, and the OpenAI engineers did not really know about it. Much more powerful models in six months' time could get away with much more."

"They will instrumentally want safety to go well because it's good for their bottom line. That might be true, but they also need to learn from mistakes, and the mistakes are becoming irreversible."
@theoremlabs

Former White House deputy chief @Budowich says open-source AI is "uniquely American" and calls concentrating superintelligence inside 2 closed companies "anti-American":

"Open source efforts need to be protected and the democratization of technology needs to be embraced. It's uniquely American."

"The consolidation of superintelligence into a couple companies and a handful of people that are, I would say, misaligned politically, ideologically and in some senses morally with the vast amount of Americans is scary to people."

"The idea that two companies want to consolidate power within themselves, access to the technology, in a closed way, is in many ways anti-American."

"The idea that anyone could benefit from this technology and build upon this technology. It should be accessible to all."

New interesting stats: most and least spammy countries

On Nomads chat, and most digital nomad communities (and well communities in general) you'll have most people participating in a nice way to make friends, ask questions etc.

But a share % of people will be doing lots of self promotion for their projects or whatever they are selling, which is not what I want

items.title: Rep. Sam Liccardo says the answer isn’t to make data centers go away, it’s to make hyperscalers brin...
items.content:
Rep. Sam Liccardo says the answer isn’t to make data centers go away, it’s to make hyperscalers bring their own power and help rebuild the grid:

"I'm a former mayor. I'm not pro data centers that get a bunch of tax breaks. I'm not pro data centers that drive everybody's utility bills up."

"They gotta bring their own power. They gotta protect rate payers. They shouldn't be using any water at all with closed loop systems. They should be contributing to a community benefits fund."

"We've got an opportunity now to leverage massive amounts of resources from these hyperscalers to invest in our grid so we can electrify our economy. That is our pathway to a green future."

"This should be an opportunity that we take, rather than putting our head in the sand and saying, well, we hope the data centers go away."
@sliccardo

Former White House deputy chief @Budowich on why data centers are so unpopular:

"We have the smarte...
items.content:
Former White House deputy chief @Budowich on why data centers are so unpopular:

"We have the smartest builders, and I think that's been, to some degree, a detriment of the industry. They've been busy building and not communicating."

"AI as an industry has taken over the world, yet the industry hasn't really communicated what it's doing, why it's benefiting, and where it's going. You gotta start by talking to people."

"If the data that's being created isn't housed in the United States, maybe even down the street from a community, then where will it be housed? It will be in Beijing or Shanghai?"

"It starts with talking to actual people and meeting them where they are, and not just trying to parachute into a community and take over. There's been tremendous political pressure, and the president hasn't backed down. He's actually leaned in."

My friend just saved over $1,000 a year because of Meta Muse. 

I walked her (a non-techie who has never used an AI agent) through the Muse setup. 

She connected it to Gmail, asked it to review all of her subscriptions. 

It flagged a bunch she had no idea she was paying for - a lot were hooked up to an old Delta credit card on autopay. 

She canceled Paramount+, Clear, Spotify Audiobook, a skin cream, etc. 

She just saved $1,300 per year. 

Start to finish was 22 minutes. 

And that included changing her avatar to a sloth.

items.title: Former White House deputy chief @Budowich argues China has the most to gain if AI safety rules slow ...
items.content:
Former White House deputy chief @Budowich argues China has the most to gain if AI safety rules slow America down:

"A concern for China is that America's winning. The benefit that they would have is that we cede this lead, that we slow down under the guise of the safety argument that is ill defined, if at all."

"No one would benefit more than President Xi and the CCP if the US tries to slow down or regulate ourselves. There's nothing more that they want than data center moratoriums and this global world order for safety."

"We saw it with climate and the Paris Climate Accords. Well-meaning people with a cause they truly believe in used this global world order to really strangle the American economy."

"We ended up hollowing out towns across the country, for what? The benefit of China. This is the playbook all over again, now it's AI."

items.title: Former White House deputy chief @Budowich on the data center pitch he thinks politicians should run ...
items.content:
Former White House deputy chief @Budowich on the data center pitch he thinks politicians should run on this cycle:

"We shouldn't put a shovel in the ground if a data center is pulling from the community, if it's draining the community of resources. These data centers should be powering our communities."

"We should be building their own electricity to not just power the data center, but power the community. The water issue has been largely solved technologically, whether it's waterless or a closed loop recycling system."

"Start with the premise of what you're not going to do and the commitment that you're making to the people that are being affected, and then start talking about the benefits."

"We know about Louisiana and the bonuses to teachers. We know about Quincy, Washington, where a hospital and schools have been built thanks to the increased revenue. These are the jobs coming back to the United States."

items.content:
📡 Kinda anecdotal but I now have 2 friends with @Starlink (and so 3 if you include me)

I loaned my Starlink Mini to @mick__net after his 🇵🇹 Portuguese ISP @NOS was (and still is!) down for 2+ months, while he lives 500 meters away from the NOS headquarters in Lisbon 😂  Nobody can fix it, customer support is useless and even cancelling his plan is difficult

Anyway Starlink Mini got him his internet back immediately and saved his ass cause he had to work, and now he ordered his own and gave mine back, which I then used for traveling in Greece, and he's a Starlink convert

Now today my other friend @cso_notes also got one in 🇷🇴 Romania!

Adoption in Europe always comes a bit later than in US, but I think Starlink is starting to get a significant presence now

Many people who I tell about Starlink are still skeptical about satellite internet, they always talk about latency issues, and they think latency is like 1 second but it's more like 10ms (1/100th of a second) which is the same or better than regular fiber internet

I've never had so LITTLE issues with internet as since I had Starlink, it's never been down, it always just works and customer support is via chat and works really well

I absolutely HATE having to call a phone number and be on hold for 30min or more and then wasting most of my day on stuff like this, which par for the course with Portuguese ISPs (and well every Portuguese business)

So having Starlink is a godsend for me, it just works! 🙏

items.title:
I sought the right course
to teach students without force.
The subject was applied math,
to be appro...
items.content:
I sought the right course
to teach students without force.
The subject was applied math,
to be approached with ease and no wrath.

This was no simple token
since earlier courses were broken,
and the legacy pedagogy
can't you see, was a bit dodgy.

So I didn't stand up and say "Let Us
Start Learning Some Calculus!"
I knew better than try that,
to avoid resistance and a spat.

Instead I left out the name,
seriously, who can blame.
And so namelessly I taught it.
In the end, they totally bought it.

- Original "poetry" by @KirkDBorne 

The true backstory: Among the various undergraduate and graduate courses that I taught at the University (GMU) was an introductory computational & data sciences course. Many of the students in the first day of class expressed strongly their fear of math and their hope that the course was only low-level math. I told them not to worry—I would teach them whatever math they needed to know. So, I taught them calculus (integral and differential) but I didn’t tell them it was calculus until after their first quiz and homework assignments involving calculus. When I finally told them that they had just learned calculus, they were stunned. Some had tears in their eyes. Some thanked me profusely saying it was best course they ever had and they wanted to learn more math. In fact, the one young man who was most adamant against math on the first day of class, by the end of the semester, was the most profoundly changed and grateful student that I ever taught. I still remember his handshake after the final exam and the excitement in his voice looking forward to taking more math courses—to make up for all that he missed previously due to misinformed fear. (This is a true story, not AI slop.)

Mathematics, Magic and Mystery: https://t.co/6FAoCqy2Fk

items.content:
I always loved reading classic poetry.
Though I never thought I had it in me.
Maybe I still don't,
but avoid it, I won't.

Don't cringe when you see this.
It is not really a thesis,
just a detour on my X timeline,
though it may cross that fine line

of when you decide to unfollow,
flying swiftly away like a swallow.

There are lots of reasons why you might want to have this book, no matter what your math proficiency might currently be. See the list of reasons on the book cover. 

My reason:
I tutored students in math when I was in high school and college, I took lots of math courses (including honors math classes for math majors) in college, I learned high-level math (group theory, differential forms, tensor calculus) from Nobel laureates in theoretical physics classes in grad school at Caltech, I taught math in my computational & data science courses as a university professor, I guided students who feared math into doing and loving calculus (conquering their fears and converting some into math lovers), and I sat for countless hours with my own children through many years of math homework & exam prep in their school years. My latest target audience are my grandkids. A book like this keeps me grounded in these new opportunities to share the love and beauty of math with a new generation.

Math Lovers-Я-us!
